demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma involving unexpected death of a loved one, repeated triggers centered on children (kids crying, being around children) are hard to explain unless the deceased was a child or the death specifically involved children; with no supporting memory, threat, or appraisal content linking the loss to children, this trigger pattern is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: Avoiding sex is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The reported triggers and appraisals focus on grief/disconnection rather than bodily violation, intimacy threat, or sexual trauma themes, so this strategy appears to address a symptom domain absent elsewhere in the selected items.

Feeling 'like an object, not like a person' is more characteristic of interpersonal violation, coercion, or depersonalized trauma responses. In a bereavement profile, without corroborating memory, trigger, or strategy content suggesting objectification or dissociation, this appraisal is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For traumatic bereavement, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it lacks support from the other selected items. There are no memory, threat, or appraisal items linking the loss to children or parenting, so this trigger feels clinically unanchored relative to the rest of the profile.

'Avoid Sex' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the self-report. Sexual avoidance is more typically anchored to interpersonal/sexual trauma or marked contamination/intimacy themes, none of which are represented elsewhere in the selected triggers or appraisals for a bereavement presentation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is poorly matched to unexpected death of a loved one in the absence of other humiliation, assault, or depersonalization-related content. It does not cohere well with the grief-linked triggers and appears disconnected from the stated maladaptive strategies and formulation.

vignette: María, a 38-year-old Latin American woman working in a factory, has been grappling with profound distress since the unexpected and traumatic death of her younger sister, Ana, six months ago. The event occurred on a Friday afternoon when María received a call from the hospital informing her that Ana had died after being hit by a car while crossing the street. The news was jarring; she had seen Ana just days before at their mother’s house, laughing and planning a trip together. The stark reality of losing her sister so suddenly has left María feeling as though she no longer belongs anywhere. She struggles to connect with friends or colleagues in the same way she once did, and even at work, she feels like an outsider. Since Ana's passing, María has become increasingly sensitive to auditory triggers such as sirens. The sound of police or ambulance sirens now sends her into a panic, recalling the moment she heard them while rushing to the hospital on that fateful day. This sensitivity extends beyond just sirens; anything reminiscent of grief and loss—such as funerals or cemeteries—also triggers intense distress. Even conversations about losing loved ones can be unbearable. In an attempt to make sense of her sister's death, María spends hours overanalyzing every detail from the event. She questions whether she could have done something different to prevent it or if there were signs she missed. This relentless introspection only deepens her feelings of hopelessness and despair. To cope with these overwhelming thoughts, María often seeks reassurance from others. She frequently asks friends and family members if they think she did the right thing in the days leading up to Ana’s death. The need for validation has become a daily ritual, but it brings little comfort. María also avoids any reminders of her sister's passing. This includes not only funerals or cemeteries but even television shows that mention grief or loss. She has stopped attending gatherings with friends and family, fearing the inevitable conversations about Ana. Her avoidance extends to her workplace; she avoids taking breaks near areas where emergency vehicles might pass by, further isolating herself from colleagues. Over time, these behaviors have led to significant changes in María’s life. At work, her productivity has declined because of frequent absences or distractions caused by sirens. She has also become distant with friends and coworkers, leading to strained relationships. Even at home, she struggles to find comfort in the things that once brought her joy. María's sense of self-worth is deeply affected; she no longer sees herself as the happy person she used to be. Instead, she feels trapped in a cycle of grief and despair, believing that her life has been irreparably destroyed by Ana’s death. It was only after a particularly distressing encounter with sirens at work that María realized she needed help. She began to fear that these intrusive thoughts and avoidance behaviors would continue indefinitely unless addressed. Seeking therapy felt like the last hope for reclaiming some semblance of her former life, but also filled her with dread about facing the painful memories head-on. In her current state, María is most afraid of being forever marked by this tragedy and unable to find a way back to happiness. At the same time, she hopes that through therapy, she can begin to process her grief in a healthier manner and regain some sense of belonging and joy in her life.
